utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. The appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, Mr. Mundis, Mr. Withopf, the Defence attorneys, the accused, and all the staff of this courtroom, without, of course, not forgetting the interpreters, the court reporters, and the security officers. We were a bit late yesterday because we had a witness who took two days instead of one, but we have a new witness for today. Could you introduce this witness, Mr. Withopf, who's going to be called this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the first witness to be called today is Peter Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Usher, will you go and bring in this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me make sure that you can hear in your own language the translation of my words. If that is so, please tell me that you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution so that we can hear your testimony today. For that purpose, I need to know your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first name is Peter. My last name is Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 25th of June, 1951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born? In which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Windsor, in England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation or profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am head of the NATO military liaison mission in Moscow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what was the position you held at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, I was the commanding officer of the 1st Battalion Coldstream Guards serving in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in court about the facts that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993, or is this the first time that you are testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified on one previous occasion, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember in which case that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the trial of Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already testified, the information I'm going to give you will be very concise. As I was saying a moment ago, you are a witness for the Prosecution. The representatives of the Prosecution are seated to your right. Following the examination-in-chief, which will be conducted by a representative of the Prosecution, the Defence attorneys, seated on your left, will have questions for you. The nature of those questions put by the Defence may be quite different to those put to you by the Prosecution. You have in front of you three Judges, who may when they consider it fit also ask you questions either to clarify certain answers that you may have given to questions put by either party or to fill in any gaps that the Judges may see. Also, you have pledged to tell the whole truth, which excludes all false testimony, and I need to remind you of something which certainly doesn't apply to you, and that is if a witness during his testimony gives evidence that could one day incriminate him, the witness may refuse to answer that question, and according to our procedure, the Chamber may compel him to answer, guaranteeing him at the same time a kind of immunity from prosecution. Those would be in brief the procedural elements of this hearing. Please try to give as complete answers as possible to the questions put to you because this is an oral proceeding and the Judges have no written documents in front of them when you are being asked questions. Hence, the importance of the answers you give to questions which are desired to establish the truth. I turn now to the representatives of the Prosecution, and I give the floor to Mr. Mundis, whom I greet once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us just a few moments ago that you are the head of the NATO mission in Moscow. In that capacity, are you a civilian or a serving member of the military?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm still a serving member of the British military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, can you please just briefly for the benefit of the Trial Chamber relate your military career from the time when you first joined the British Army up until the present day.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I joined the British Army in 1972, on leaving university. I joined the Coldstream Guards, which is an infantry regiment and I've served in that regiment since that time. I've served overseas in the army of the Sultan of Oman, I served in Hong Kong, many times in Germany, Belgium. I spent a year in Australia. And I have commanded troops in Northern Ireland and then in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the time period in 1993, did your unit or part of your unit serve in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The whole of my battalion served in Bosnia from the -- about the 12th of November or early November 1993 through until the beginning of May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during this deployment from early November 1993 until the beginning of May 1994, what was your capacity in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was the commanding officer of the battalion based in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, for the record, sir, the name of the battalion that you commanded in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 1st Battalion, the Coldstream Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, can you please tell us what training or briefing you and your unit received prior to your deployment to Bosnia in early November 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The unit that I commanded was principally an armoured infantry unit, and so the main part of the training for the first half of 1993 concerned the conversion of the battalion to become fully capable as armoured infantry. We were then warned in May of 1993 that we would become the third British battalion to serve in Bosnia, and our training then moved from armoured infantry training, the conventional training, to specialised training in advance of that tour in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what -- what were the aspects of this specialised training that your battalion received prior to this deployment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a specialised training package designed by the British military authorities based to some extent at first on our experience in Northern Ireland, in order to give officers and soldiers the right background information and whatever specialised training was needed, for example, in negotiation skills and so forth, that would be needed during our deployment in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what type of briefings, if any, did you receive about the situation on the ground in Bosnia, the parties to the conflict in Bosnia, et cetera, prior to your deployment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were a number of briefings given, some given to all the troops to try and give them a sense of what the situation was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and more detailed briefings were given to officers and those who were going to be dealing with military information, which was the term then used for what we would perhaps more conventionally call intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, how was this military information that you've referred to, what was that -- what was done with that information? How was it compiled, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Military information that was compiled and that was available to the battalion was collected by the assets that belonged to the battalion on the ground in Central Bosnia. Within the battalion, we had, I think, ten specialist liaison officers, young officers, mostly captains. Their job was to move around the battalion area, speaking to the military authorities of the warring parties, and to other civil leaders to try to discover what was going on in the area. The purpose of collecting this information was to give the battalion authorities, myself in particular, enough information for us to make sensible judgements on when the humanitarian task that was our principal task was safe to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'll return to these military-information process in just a few moments. But before I do, did -- let me ask you a couple of other questions: Did the 1st Battalion of the Coldstream Guards replace or relieve any other British battalions upon arrival in Bosnia in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed. We were, as I said before, the third British battalion to deploy to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The first had been the Cheshire Regiment. And we replaced the second, which was the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So sir, what was the responsibility of the 1st Battalion of the Coldstream Guards or the British battalion at the time your unit deployed there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The area of responsibility stretched from the south of the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia through Tomislavgrad, through the area between Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, and then north to the area between Travnik and Vitez and Zenica. And it later extended up -- further up the Bosna Valley towards Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time your battalion deployed to Bosnia, can you briefly tell us how many men you had, how those men were organised into lower-level units, and what type of military equipment you deployed with.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The battalion was in fact a battalion group, rather than a battalion as such, because it had in addition to the normal three rifle companies and a support company, we also had one squadron of the Light Dragoons, a medium reconnaissance regiment, attached to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many men were in the battalion and what type of equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The number of people varied, obviously, but I would think -- around about 700 to 750 at any one time; certainly about 50 officers. The infantry part of the battalion was principally equipped with the Warrior armoured fighting vehicle, which weighs 27 tonnes, and the medium reconnaissance regiment was armed -- elements were armed or equipped with Scimitar, which is a light reconnaissance -- tracked reconnaissance vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what -- can you briefly describe for us what was the primary mission of your battalion at the time and what were the subcomponents of that mission. What were you there to do?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The mission of the battalion was never formally given to us, strangely, but the mission that we inherited from the previous battalion was to create the conditions for the delivery of humanitarian aid into and within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us -- you've told us a little bit about the military information that you were able to receive from your liaison officers and other sources. Can you briefly tell us how information was received by yourself, how -- in other words, how the information came up the chain of command and then how you disseminated that information back down the chain to the various members of your battalion.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I may, I'd start by saying that nothing came from above us. We had no information given to us from higher headquarters within the UN system. So all the information we needed, we had to collect ourselves. The principal means of collecting information was through the ten or so liaison officers, who worked closely with the headquarters, normally at brigade level, of the warring factions, and the company commanders themselves, who would be expected to crisis-manage as best they could by visiting places where there were incidents going on and by trying to negotiate the opening of -- in particular, of crossing points over front lines. There were a number of other organisations working in our area. The UN military observers arrived early in our time, and the European Community Monitoring Mission. Our aim was to bring together - and this was normally done at the end of each day during a conference that we held at about 6.00 each day - our aim was to bring together today's current information, to talk about it. And then the military information officer would put all that information together that evening in a military-information summary, a milinfosum, and that was then passed further up the chain in the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that you didn't receive any information coming from above you, from any higher headquarters within the UN. Did you, however, receive any type of turnover briefing from any of the senior leadership of the Prince of Wales' Own?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We had an extensive handover from the Prince of Wales' Own. Each of the company commanders and myself were in theatre with our counterparts from the preceding battalion for, on average, between five and seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of information you received during that turnover or these turnover briefings concerning the parties to the conflict that were in the area of responsibility for which your battalion assumed responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The situation, of course, was very complex. And when we arrived in -- around about the 10th of November, there was, of course, a crisis in that there were no humanitarian aid being delivered. There had been a -- I think a Norwegian had been killed in late October to the south of Vitez in a convoy. So the situation was confused, but there were inevitably maps marked up showing what the Prince of Wales' Own believed to be the situation on the ground and which warring faction units, brigades, and so forth were located in specific areas. And so although the situation was confused, we felt that normally we had sufficient information to be able to make reasonable judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at the time you arrived, what were the warring factions that were operating in your AOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The principal parties with whom we were obliged to deal were the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, the Croat forces. The Bosnian Serb army was also in evidence around the area and held the area beyond Turbe and Travnik but was not in any sense influencing our principal mission, which, as I would remind you, was to bring or in a safe manner convoys from Split through Tomislavgrad up through Gornji Vakuf and Vitez and to the principal distribution depot in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, were there -- other than your humanitarian aid mission, were there other issues that arose during the first, say, month or month and a half that you were in Bosnia that more or less fell outside of your primary mission but which you otherwise dealt with?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We tried as far as possible not to get dragged into issues that were not linked to our principal task, ensuring the safe delivery of humanitarian assistance of all sorts within Central Bosnia. It was perhaps tempting to get involved in the war, but obviously it was somebody else's war and we -- I was insistent that we should concentrate on what we'd been sent there to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about what you personally did while you were on the ground in Bosnia. In other words, did you remain in your headquarters? Did you get out and travel around the area? What primarily were you doing during the roughly six months that you were deployed in Bosnia on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Clearly I had a very competent team around me in the headquarters in Vitez, and this enabled me to travel extensively and daily. I was travelling around my battalion area visiting the companies and also visiting the commanders of the warring factions in order to gain my own impression of what was going on and in order to negotiate the freer movement of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During these times that you were moving around, were you also in any way compiling any type of information?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Of course. Whenever I went to meetings, I would make short notes before I went to the meetings as to topics that I wished and needed to cover, and then I would make short notes afterwards to remind myself of what had happened so that I could brief people at the 6.00 meeting in the evening and could include the pertinent points in the daily milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These short notes that you took or either contemporaneously or shortly afterwards to remind yourself, what did you do with those notes?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I kept the notebooks as such, but I also -- at the end of each day, I would compile a diary of sorts to tell my -- try and remind myself of the principal points of the day in order that I should have some record later on. This was the advice I'd been given by the commanding officer of the 1st British Battalion, Colonel Bob Stewart of the Cheshires, who said it was vital that one should keep a diary so that a very busy situation should at least have some structure to it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown what has been marked as PTW3085.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you have before you a document which we've marked PTW3085. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This document is a document I compiled in 1995 whilst in a less than spectacularly interesting job in the Ministry of Defence, and it is a summary of the diary entries from my diaries during the winter of 1993/1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it from that answer, sir, that you took your previous written diaries and transcribed them, if you will, or typed them into this document.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Since creating this document in 1995, have you had a chance to review it or read through it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, does it accurately reflect the situation as you recorded it in late 1993, early 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is my best attempt -- a deliberate attempt to bring together the facts as best I can from -- not only from my own diary but from other documents that I retained at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender PTW3085 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President. Mr. President, I was wondering why my learned friend was using this document and for what purpose he's showing the document to the witness. The Defence feels that there's -- that this document cannot be admitted into evidence. As you have said on several occasions, Mr. President, this is an oral procedure and the document proposed by the Prosecution is a collection of personal documents, a diary compiled during the events. It is not a personal diary, in fact. It's a summary of several personal notes compiled during the events but produced in 1995, which means two years after the events, and the witness appearing before this Chamber -- all the witnesses have compiled notes of one kind or another and when a witness appears, he is never asked to produce those personal documents. When a witness comes to testify orally, he is there to do so, and I thought that my learned friend wanted to use these documents to refresh the memory of the witness, which is a different thing altogether, and in that case the Defence has no objection. However, we have here the primary source of information, a witness here in the court who can tell us what he saw, what he knows, and how he formed his opinion. So why would we need to tender a document when we have the primary source in front of us? And if we look at the date of these notes, the witness speaks about certain events that took place during the preparation of his battalion for deployment in Bosnia, and then he goes on to talk of events, most of which took place outside the scope of the indictment. The witness arrived in Bosnia in November 1993, whereas the indictment period ends on the 4th of November, 1993. For the accused that I represent, it ends the 31st of October -- that is, the 1st of November, when his position ended. Therefore, these are notes of this witness who can give us his opinion orally, and we don't think that the Chamber would benefit in any way in having these notes after the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Prosecution for their response to the observations made by the Defence, the Chamber notes that this document is a document that was drafted by the witness who is present today. This document begins on the 30th of December, 1992, and the last date is the 14th to the 20th of May, 1994. As has been indicated by the Defence, there is reference to periods which are not covered by the indictment and which refer to a period when the witness was not on the spot. Therefore, this document can be useful to us only with respect to the period from November 1993 to March 1994. In the opinion of the Chamber and the President of the Chamber, it would appear that the Defence is asking this document to be admitted, whereas the questions that may be usefully put and this document produced to refresh the memory of the witness have not been put to the witness. Do you intend to ask questions about certain sentences appearing in this document? The most logical procedure, juridically, would be to ask the witness questions regarding the periods referred to in this document; the witness could confirm or deny certain statements in the document, and after that you could ask for the document to be tendered. So I give the floor to Mr. Mundis to tell me whether he intends to ask questions of this witness about parts of the document or other questions and ask -- does he intend to ask this document to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I respond both to Your Honour's questions and those of my learned colleague from the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic, perhaps we should hear from the Defence for Mr. Kubura, if they have any further observations to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I was waiting to hear what the Prosecution was going to say first about how they intend to use the document, because my submission would be that it would be preferable that the document at this stage only be marked for identification and that once the witness is asked questions a determination can be made, depending on what answers are made, whether it's necessary for the document to be admitted. If the witness is to be asked questions about the period which is inevitable, as Mr. Bourgon has said, the best evidence would be the oral evidence that the witness is able to give. If it's necessary to refer to a diary in order to refresh his memory, then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that could be done upon application being made by the Prosecution. And at that stage, if it is necessary for parts of the document to be admitted, depending on what the answers are, that could be the course of action that is then considered. The danger of admitting the document wholesale, as Your Honours have indicated, is one, that it covers periods that are not in the indictment, firstly; and secondly, it can become a self-serving document, in the sense that the witness's oral testimony is backed up or supported by the document or vice versa. Usually in common-law jurisdictions a document that simply serves to confirm the evidence that the witness is able to give is not admissible. And it's for that reason that we would suggest that the document first be marked for identification and the evidence be given and then a determination be made thereafter if it's at all necessary to admit the document into evidence. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Allow me to make just a few preliminary comments prior to proceeding. First of all, clearly, the Prosecution has no intention of relying on any of the material contained in this diary after March 1994, that is, with respect to the material after the indictment period with respect to both accused. Second, the diary clearly reflects contemporaneous information, that is, information which the witness compiled at the time, and although it was typed up only subsequently, it still, the Prosecution submits, reflects what the witness experienced on a day-to-day basis. And for that reason, Mr. President, there might be aspects of this diary which are more detailed or perhaps even more accurate than recollections of the witness sitting here in the courtroom some ten years after the events in question. Third, Mr. President, in fact the Prosecution will be asking the witness some additional questions, some of which are covered in this diary, and for that reason the Prosecution would agree to a process whereby the document is simply marked for identification at this point in time and we can discuss the admissibility of the document perhaps at the end of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us give this document a number, to be marked for identification, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P107, Your Honours, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If that document has not been retrieved from the witness, I would ask that it -- no, no, not that it be shown to the witness, that it be taken away from the witness. Thank you. I would ask at this point in time that the witness be shown P378.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, you have before you Prosecution Exhibit 378. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This document is an assessment made by the military-information cell of my battalion, the 1st Battalion Coldstream Guards. It's been made by the military information officer, Captain Burrows -- I think his name is given. And Corporal -- Sergeant Brown has made it for Captain Burrows, who was his boss. It is a compilation and an assessment based on the tactical-level information gathered by our predecessor battalions and, indeed, by the Coldstream Guards during the initial period of our time in Central Bosnia. It reflects an attempt to put some structure and substance to the organisation of the 3rd and 6th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, given that those organisations were not exactly forthcoming with information of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what was the purpose of producing the document which we refer to here as P378?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The purpose is to try to assess the combat capability of the -- of these Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formations in and around the Vitez area, which was the central part of my battalion's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know during the time period, in particular from November 1993 through December 1993, what unit or units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were in and around the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This document as such is the best indication that we had, and indeed that I would have today, of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the time period that you were in Bosnia, how much interaction did you have with the leaders of either the HVO units or the ABiH units that were in your AOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- with the leadership of the 3rd Corps, for example, I would estimate that I met with General Alagic on probably about 20 occasions during the six months that I was in Central Bosnia. With -- and, on the other hand, with the HVO, a similar number of times, either with Colonel Blaskic, as he was then, or with Colonel Filipovic, his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know or do you have a rough approximation as to when General Alagic assumed command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just after I arrived - I can't recall the date without reference to the -- to my diary - I met then-Colonel Alagic, General Hadzihasanovic and others in the headquarters of the 3rd Corps, and I was informed that this was part of the handover process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us, sir, that there were about 20 occasions during the six months that you were in Central Bosnia when you met with General Alagic. Do you recall some of the subjects that were discussed with General Alagic particularly in the first month or two months, that is, November/December 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The principal subjects that I was covering with him and indeed with his Croat counterparts were the difficulties, indeed the problems, of opening the front lines in order to allow for the arrival in Central Bosnia of convoys which were stacking up in Metkovic and elsewhere to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall other than discussions about these principal subjects, that is, convoys and the whatnot, any other subjects that you discussed with Colonel or General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were understandable nervousness on the part of not only the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but indeed on the part of the United Nations forces concerning the potential demolition of the explosives factory, the Vitezit factory near Vitez. And there were other issues that were raised, in particular the disappearance of Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you can recall about the disappearance of Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, as I recall, was one of four people who were seized in Travnik and effectively disappeared for a while. As I recall, I was given a report by my -- one of my liaison officers about this to -- trying to summarise what we thought what we knew about the situation. And then I received a letter, as did many other international authorities in the area, from Mr. Popovic's wife asking for support in freeing her husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as a result of this letter and this information that was coming to you from, among others, one of your liaison officers, what steps did you take to determine what had happened to Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I raised this issue with Colonel Alagic, as he was then, because I felt that it needed to be raised. I didn't know much about the details. I hoped that he would be able to give me some news, I hoped good news, concerning the well-being of Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you discovered or what you were able to determine based on these discussions with Colonel Alagic about Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Colonel Alagic accepted or admitted that he knew Mrs. Popovic, that this was not just a stranger who had written a letter; but he was unable to give me any good news about the well-being of Mr. Popovic. Indeed, he suggested that there was not going to be any good news about Mr. Popovic and that he would prefer to give no answer to Mrs. Popovic rather than have to tell her a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- during the remaining part of your tour in Central Bosnia, did the subject of Mr. Popovic come up on any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I recall, it didn't. It subsided. I'm not sure what the final outcome of the story was, although I have a strong suspicion that it was a sad outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown three documents, perhaps one at a time, those documents being Prosecution Exhibits 379, 380, and 381. Perhaps if we could start with 379, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you have before you Prosecution Exhibit 379, which consists of four pages. Are you familiar with the basically three documents that are together as Prosecution Exhibit 379?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what these documents are.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These documents are a letter from Captain Guinness, who was the liaison officer dealing with the area of Travnik, talking about the fact that hostages were being held, according to the letter, by Mujahedin; part of a military information summary dated the 1st of December discussing the same issue; and my own letter, which I sent covering these two documents to the chief of staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Kiseljak, General Ramsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask now -- with the assistance of the usher that you now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 380. Sir, are you familiar with Prosecution Exhibit 380?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you looking, sir, at the English translation or at the original in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am looking at the English translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could take a look, sir, at the B/C/S version of this document. Sir, do you read any or understand any Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Only a small amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S version of this document, on the bottom left-hand corner do you see any handwritten markings?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see my own initials on the bottom left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you in fact produce a copy of this document or this document to the investigator of the Tribunal when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I'd ask you that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 381, which consists of about ten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with Prosecution Exhibit 381?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is an extract from my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could, please, flip through that. Are there any other documents in this bundle? And if so, can you please tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There is an initial draft of a report about a meeting between Commander Alagic and myself on the 15th of December, 1993, and there is a report that came from Bosnia-Herzegovina command about the same -- about a meeting on the 16th of December at Visoko. All the other documents are from my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you make reference to an initial draft of a report, would that be those pages within Prosecution Exhibit 381 that begin with -- or the first page of which is -- appears to be your letterhead?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Those documents can be returned to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- sir, these documents have made reference to the Mujahedin. Did you on any occasion discuss with senior leaders of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina the issue of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not directly as Mujahedin. There was often -- reference was made by senior leaders to so-called uncontrolled elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was your interpretation of "uncontrolled elements"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Given the -- the clearly well-organised, well-structured form of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was always, I have to say, sceptical about the existence of so-called uncontrolled elements. They seemed to pop up and disappear in a rather convenient fashion from the perspective of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please elaborate for us what you mean when you say "the clearly well-organised, well-structured form of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." What does that mean? How did you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Along with the -- indeed, with the other two warring parties, all the warring parties that we dealt with in Central Bosnia were what I would describe as well structured and relatively well-organised military forces. They all had weaknesses, in the case of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the weaknesses were clearly to do with the amount of equipment, war-fighting equipment that they had. But in my view, the structures from the central general staff, as it were, down through the corps level and ops groups and brigades and so forth and down to battalion level, this was a conventionally and sensibly structured organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your dealings with Colonel Alagic or others, other leaders of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, did you get a sense as to issues relating to command and control within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At no time during my time in Central Bosnia during those six months, did I ever have a feeling that this was an organisation that was anything other than well organised and, indeed, well commanded, given the stringencies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of communications equipment did the 3rd Corps have available to them, if you are aware of any such equipment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The only occasion when I was very clearly aware of the equipment involved was an incident in December when I noticed that a message was being sent on a H -- a high-frequency radio set that was identical to the high-frequency sets that had been issued to my battalion. These were produced by the British company Racal, and I understood had been manufactured under licence during the time the former -- of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with, at least on a basic level, the capabilities of these high-frequency Racal radios?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The advantage of these high-frequency radios that they work well in mountainous conditions, unlike most of the radio that is we had that were very high frequency and had great limitations in mountainous conditions. The actual use of these radios by the BiH on the occasion in question, it was clear they were able to send a complex message from Pavlovica, halfway between Vitez and Gornji Vakuf. The message was sent to Bugojno and was received and presumably decrypted there before I could reach Bugojno. So this suggested to me a well-organized and smooth-running communication system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, I have a couple of follow-on questions based on your last answer. You alluded to a message being decrypted. Can you elaborate upon what you meant by "decrypted," particularly as it relates to the capabilities of the Racal high-frequency radio system.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All I can say, if I may, is that it would be normal for military communications containing sensitive information, which indeed this one did - this one was a message about the -- a Croat convoy that had been found carrying contraband military equipment - it would be normal for this information to be sent other than in clear language and it would therefore need to be deciphered at the far end before it could be actioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if I understand you, sir, this radio -- this Racal high-frequency radio system was capable of sending secure information.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The information would have to be encoded before it would be sent. In that sense, it would be secured. It's not an automatically secure radio system, as per very modern radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I have a question, then, about this incident that you've told us about where you became aware that the ABiH had this type of system. You made reference to a message being sent to Bugojno which was received before you got to Bugojno. Can you just describe briefly what happened on that day so that we understand the situation as it unfolded.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This was an incident concerning the movement of two convoys; one, a Croat-sponsored convoy; one, a BiH-sponsored convoy. These were moving into Central Bosnia carrying humanitarian assistance in the period immediately before Christmas in 1993. The complexities of this and the security aspects were enormous and I involved myself, and most of my senior commanders worked on the non-stop for about five days to try and achieve the successful arrival of both convoys in Central Bosnia. The unfortunate fact was that the Croat convoy, when it was searched by the ARBiH was found contained military contraband and detonators and a number of other bits of war-fighting equipment, and this was clearly in contravention of the agreement that had been made concerning the reciprocal movement of these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as a result of this incident, you then became involved in discussions concerning this convoy and that's how you became aware of this radio system.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Absolutely. The decision was that the leader of the Croat convoy should be sent from Pavlovica to Bugojno, where there would be -- a, ARBiH decision would be made on whether or not the convoy could continue. And in the time it took us to get from Pavlovica, effectively on the top of the mountain, down to Bugojno, this message had been sent by the ARBiH element at Pavlovica and had been received and action had been prepared in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the speakers to make pauses between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, I have just a few more questions for you. You've told us about a meeting that you attended shortly after your arrival with both Colonel Alagic and General Hadzihasanovic being present. Other than that occasion -- on how many other occasions, that would be -- on how many other occasions did you have any dealing with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I only had occasion to meet him I think on two other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what -- in what capacity was General Hadzihasanovic serving on those two subsequent occasions, that is, after November 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I understood it, he was the chief of staff of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, sir, on any occasion have the opportunity of meeting with Amir Kubura?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that on any occasion I met with Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Defence for the cross-examination. The Judges will have questions too, but they'll put them later. Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. We had a brief meeting yesterday, but I will introduce myself nevertheless. I am Edina Residovic, and with my colleague Stephane Bourgon and legal assistant Mirna Milanovic, I am representing General Hadzihasanovic. Is it true, General, that before today's testimony in this Trial Chamber you gave two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, on the 5th and 7th of June, 1998 and on the 18th and 19th of September, 2001? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the President of the Trial Chamber, you confirm that you testified in this Tribunal in the Kordic case and that was at the end of January 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but it -- I'm sure that's when it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you testified today, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina from November 1993 to May 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of your professional duties, you spent most of your time as a staff officer, that is, you were working in the staff of various military units or you were the deputy commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was a normal infantry officer up until the time that I commanded the battalion. Since that time, I have been employed as a General Staff officer. And before becoming a commanding officer of a battalion, I also spent some time as an officer on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the position of battalion commander in Bosnia and Herzegovina was your first command role in the British Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I had commanded troops at platoon level, company level and battalion level in Northern Ireland before taking my battalion to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You took over your duties in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 8th of November, when you replaced the Prince of Wales' battalion within the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you also said that you became battalion commander in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that time on, you underwent various types of trainings and you trained your battalion -- you exercised your battalion at the base in Germany; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In August until the end of December, I was commanding the battalion in Northern Ireland. We then moved back to Germany and started training at the beginning of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you learnt that you would be deployed in Bosnia, you prepared the battalion according to a special programme to prepare your troops for their mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a specific package of training designed by the British military for battalions such as my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your battalion, before being given this assignment, was considered to be a highly professional military unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Before I took over the command of the battalion, it had recently returned from involvement in the Gulf War in Iraq, so I think it would be considered to be a very professional organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers that were members of your battalion were professional soldiers with considerable experience and military knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: For over 40 years all members of the British Army have been volunteers and, therefore, professional military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in spite of that, your assignment in Bosnia and Herzegovina was seen as being an additional challenge which required additional training and a specific package of training, as you yourself have said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is typical. In advance of all operational deployments, units will be given specific to that -- training that is specific to that operational deployment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that from the moment you took over command of the battalion, for a year in practice in Northern Ireland and during various other training courses you continued the professional advancement of your battalion to make quite sure that they would be capable of fulfilling the mission assigned to them?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is very much the task of a commanding officer, to make sure that all his men are ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your vast professional and theoretical knowledge and experience, would you agree with me, General, if I say that you had to train not a battalion but a corps for performing certain military assignments -- should you have had to train a corps, you would have needed much more time than you needed for preparing your battalion? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The complexities of training a corps would obviously be greater than those of training a battalion group, and because of the complexities, it would be likely -- under the British system, you would certainly need longer in order to reach those higher levels of command and integrate the training throughout them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When in November 1993, General, you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you came to an area that coincided with the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps even before, but then certainly, you must have learnt that the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been in the process of formation for less than a year. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think I probably was aware at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also must have known that the corps was being formed under extremely unfavourable conditions for the formation of a military unit; that is, under the difficult conditions of a battle being waged on two fronts.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Clearly the conditions were difficult, but actual structure of a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. corps in itself is not anything that's particularly unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to questions from my learned friend, General, you mentioned that to the north of your area of responsibility there was the front line with the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, which did not have a significant impact on your own mission. Do you recollect saying that today?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, during the performance of your duties, you knew that the front line against the Serbs extended over some 250 to 300 kilometres and that it engaged the 3rd Corps and its commander significantly in view of the combat operations that were going on along that front.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I accept that that was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the light of what you said in this Trial Chamber regarding the preparations for your own battalion to perform its assignment in an area of combat activities, I think you will agree with me if I say that Enver Hadzihasanovic's task, as the commander of the 3rd Corps - to create the 3rd Corps, to structure the units consisting of some 30.000 men who were not professional soldiers, unlike your own troops, and at the same time to wage war on two fronts - was an exceptionally difficult military assignment. Would you agree with this statement of mine?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I agree. It must have been an exceptional assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Proceeding from your own military knowledge and considerable experience, could you agree with me in saying that the formation of a unit and especially of a corps is a process that cannot be done through issuing an order or writing an order on the formation of a corps and its structure?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I would disagree to some extent. I think that it -- there is an aspect of this where it's a case of somebody setting down the structure, authorising the start of a process. And thereafter the difficulties lie not in creating the structure and identifying the process, the difficulties lie in delivering what has been identified as the requirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was just what I expected to hear from you. Actually, one can say that a corps is established by an order or by the appointment or the formation of a structure, but it starts to function properly when all the elements of that structure are actually put into practice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's true to say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I would like to ask you, General, to tell me whether I am right in saying that the realisation of the intention as to what the corps should be like and how it should operate is a process that differs at the beginning from what the attained goal looks like a year later.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it's reasonable to expect that things will evolve during the course of that year, but I would hope that the plan at the beginning would have been a sound plan and that most of the elements would have been delivered as envisaged at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived in November 1993, and you told Their Honours what your assessment of the corps was at the time you arrived. Would you agree with me if I say that this was a far more developed and better organised structure in practice than it had been a year prior to that when the decision had been made to form the corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't speak for what the decision had been a year earlier, but I do consider that the situation on the ground, which consisted of a number of brigades working through operations groups to corps headquarters and then on to the higher headquarters, had all the structural strength of a proper corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, what you just said -- would I be right in saying that you really cannot know the kind of problems the corps had from January to October, prior to your arrival, and it is only after that that you can testify about the structure of the corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed here that before coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina you received some basic information regarding the military situation in the area you were being assigned to and you also had a general assessment of the situation on the ground conveyed to you by the previous battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you already were aware that it was one of the six republics of the former SFRY which had been granted independence and which had become a UN member in 1992; were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also probably knew that Bosnia and Herzegovina on the day of its recognition on the 6th of April, 1992 was attacked by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb forces. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had read news reports concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an experienced military man, you also knew that Bosnia and Herzegovina went to war without having any armed force prior to that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is no doubt correct, but of course there were many people within that force who had received military education of one sort or another during the previous Yugoslav era.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question from my learned friend, you said that you were actually never given a military assignment but that you took over the assignments passed on to you by the Prince of Wales' battalion, which was your predecessor in the area, and those were the assignments that you carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. I asked the British brigadier in Split if he wished to give me detailed orders, and his reaction was that the situation changed so quickly in Central Bosnia that if he was to write an operation order, it would be redundant before it could be implemented. And so he just told me to carry on doing what he felt my predecessor battalion had been doing very successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, General, even though you were not given any such assignment, you knew that the Security Council had passed a resolution on the formation of UN Protection Forces, known as UNPROFOR, whose mandate was regulated by Resolution 776 of the Security Council. Were you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was familiar with that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General, because I only have one copy of that resolution with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to ask this resolution to be given to the General, and would you please place it on the overhead projector so that all of us could see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: By this resolution, the mandate was actually defined of UNPROFOR, that is, "to secure protection of land convoys of humanitarian aid organised by the UNHCR and also to protect the International Red Cross mission in the exchange of prisoners when they request such aid and when such assistance is approved." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will ask this resolution to be marked for identification, though I do believe it already exists as an exhibit. But as we don't have a sufficient number of copies, we will tender it into evidence once we have copied it during the break and provided copies to all participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. Can we hear the Prosecution regarding this document, Resolution 776.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to UN Security Council resolutions being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let's give it an exhibit number, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DH127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps now would be the appropriate time for the break and we can organise ourselves in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have the break, you haven't attached a B/C/S translation of that resolution. You probably translated it for the benefit of the accused. Madam Registrar, can you remind us of the exhibit number that you just gave to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DH127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is 10.30. We're going to have the customary break, and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume the hearing. I would like to give the floor to the counsel for Defence to continue the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, before the break, we saw the resolution of the Security Council. Are you aware that following the adoption of that resolution there was an enlargement of the terms of office of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina but your basic mission remained within the mandate of offering support to the humanitarian convoys there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. The mission that we believed ourselves to have conformed closely -- indeed, is exactly that in the UN Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, General, not at any moment while conducting your mission you had no authority stemming from Chapter 7 of the UN charter; that is to say, that you were not able to establish peace in the area and to use force to that end. But you behaved in accordance with the provisions of Charter 7, you were support of the humanitarian aid mission.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That mission that you were performing did not make it possible for you or give you the right to influence the rights and the positions of the parties in the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was notice in our interest to do so. We simply wished to conduct operations in line with the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were able to conduct a mission only if there was an agreement on both parties involved in the conflict in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. It's particularly the case, for example, with the crossing of front lines. Both parties, warring parties, needed to be in accord with our plan before we would risk pushing convoys, largely manned with civilians, across front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your soldiers were able to use force only in the event of legitimate defence and according to a specific procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was largely a matter of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The parties were duty-bound to offer you a certain support, but they were never under the obligation to enable you to access their military secrets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. And I would say that all the parties were very good at what we would describe as operational security.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whilst performing your duties, you did your best to avoid activities which the parties to the conflict could assess as interference in the positions of one of the parties or of favouring one of the parties in the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Theoretically that may have been correct, but in reality there were activities going on around us which demanded our interest. In particular, I would mention accusations by one party against another party of massacres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your battalion, however -- though as you had explained, obtained some information, this was not done in a way as usually battalions to engaged in a conflict should obtain. You did not act as a battalion in conflict and you did not procure intelligence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The only intelligence that we were able to gather was through human means, through trying to first gain the trust of people and then to ask their opinions and for whatever they wished to tell us about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us the procedure whereby you drafted your daily reports, milinfosums. Is it true that you had a soldier in charge of this and who drafted the report on the basis of information received by the liaison officer or officers which were on the ground in the field with the companies? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In each company headquarters and then at the higher level at battalion headquarters, there were officers and soldiers responsible for the collation of military information and for passing this up the system, further up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that the information you compiled as milinfosums, you did not give to the parties in the conflict nor did the parties have access to this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This was very much viewed as confidential information that had been given to us in trust by one party or other, and we certainly would never have dreamt of exposing what one party had said to the other party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the parties to the conflict, either the command of the ABiH army or the HVO, received only that information which were given to them at meetings, directly.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think we probably passed very little information to them that was not information strictly about the business of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, is it true, General, that you nor the members of other international organisations, you did not have access to the orders from the staff of the Supreme Command of ABiH or the Main Staff of the HVO to lower-level units?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Normally this was not -- we did not have access to such information, although on one occasion we did receive via a humanitarian organisation an order from General Delic that had been passed to three of the corps headquarters, which reflected what we considered to be the chain of command at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General. I have a warning. Someone is suggesting something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We have just asked you whether it was your possibility -- your ability to gain possession or come to orders that went from the higher levels of corps to the lower units. Is it also true that you did not have access to confidential military information which the parties to the conflict had in their possession?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We had no access to any information other than the information that people gave willingly to us, either from other UN or international organisations or indeed from the warring parties. But on a routine basis, the answer is no, we had no access.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In response to the question of the Prosecution, you said that the aim of the information that you collected was to assess the combat readiness in order to provide for the security of your mission. Was that the purpose of the information that you collected?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that "combat readiness" is a technical term and is probably the wrong description. We needed information about the warring -- the situation of the war in order that we could make informed decisions on the safety or otherwise of the movement of humanitarian aid. That was the principal purpose of the military-information system that we had and the military information system existed only to serve the command element.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if I understood you well, that you were not interested in information or you were not predominantly interested in information that would inform you of the true structure of the army and of its combat readiness to conduct military operation that that army had within its competence.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We did not have the need that an opposing force would have had for as full a picture as possible for any one of the warring parties. Our only requirement for information was to support decisions that we were making to implement the mandate given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also briefly explained the way in which you collected that information. You described the number of soldiers you had in the field. And I would like to ask you now whether it is true, General, that the means that you used to collect that information were limited to personal observation from meetings with military officers or civilian bodies or other persons who would be able to give you relevant information for your mission on the ground.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. We had no technical means of gathering intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And actually, by using technical electronic means or satellites would have been -- made it possible for you to receive more secure information that you were collecting.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no doubt that technical, electronic and other means were being deployed, but the information gathered in that way was not in any sense passed down to the battalion level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of our talk yesterday, General, if you recall, you said that your intelligent agents were tactical intelligent agents. General, could you perhaps, if you remember -- if you recall your statement, could you explain to us what tactical information was -- what a tactical intelligent agent is.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What I was suggesting by referring to it as "tactical intelligence" was that this was information that could be processed into intelligence that was useful at the battalion level and, therefore, at the tactical level. This would -- this was information that would affect our ability to act today or maybe tomorrow. This was not long-term intelligence that we were seeking. It was simply the information necessary to ensure safe humanitarian operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, General, you told us that the information that you possessed were only the best indication of the situation with regard to the purpose of your mission. Is it true that this is the way in which you answered our question?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly how I answered your question, but I would repeat that we only needed information in order to make the best possible decisions for tactical operations. Those are our own operations. We did not need and did not seek information for its own sake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were aware of the fact that your information depended on the reliability of the sources of that information provided to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Of course we could only use the information that was given to us, but we were using information that was given to us by both of the warring parties in Central Bosnia, that is the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat military, and we were using our best judgement to assess whether the information we had been given was reliable and probable or whether this was sometimes perhaps disinformation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If then or today you were confronted with an information which was far more important or far more reliable, you are sure that some of the conclusions of your information would be different than the conclusions that you had at the time. Would this be the right approach to the -- to what you have just said now?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no doubt at all that with hindsight and with the availability of much more information our assessments would probably have been different.
