But the reality of life as a commander in the field is that you cannot wait for all the information, you have to take what you have. You have to make a sensible assessment, and then you have to make decisions based on that. There is always a risk that you are making a decision on poor information, but you need as much information as you can possibly acquire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you, so to speak, were confident that the information you received from the officer in Split was correct because the events on the field were evolving so quickly that very often an information would become incomplete or unreliable and information as to subsequent events would come from other sources which were accessible to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My British commander in Split, who was a brigadier, he, I think, appreciated that it was very difficult for him to make decisions based on the Adriatic coast and removed from the situation, and in the traditional British way, the initiative was passed to commanders on the ground, in this case myself in Vitez, and we were trusted to make the best decisions. If we made a poor decision, it would be our funeral; if we made a good one, then they would congratulate us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You took over considerable responsibility, but I believe that you can be satisfied with your mission. In connection with the information that we have just discussed, I would like you to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 378 so as to be able to ask you some additional questions. Along with this document, there is an analysis of the activities of the 3rd Corps. And on page 2, you can see the structure under point d about the Operations Group Bosnia. Is that the document you have before you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have said, this document was compiled on the basis of your knowledge after a month's presence in the area, but also on the basis of information that the previous BritBat battalions had in their possession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This assessment was the best assessment that was possible by the British Battalion after about one year in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You in fact answered in response to my question that there were -- that if you had other information, the assessment would have not been the same. In other words, if you had orders of the Supreme Command or the 3rd Corps that the 301st, 303rd Brigade were manoeuvre units within the structure 3rd Corps and that the conclusion, that it is only about the 7th Muslim Brigade as a manoeuvre unit, would not have been the same as what is written here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I and my staff had had that information, I'm sure we would have made a different assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you another question in that connection, since your answers very correctly reflect an assessment of the information that you had in your possession and the possibilities thereof to conclude about the structure of the corps or other issues contained in your report. You can see under d that you -- that one of the brigades within the Operations Group Bosna is the 301st Brigade. If you had the development plan of the 3rd Corps where it says that the third group that wishes to have as a manoeuvre unit a mechanised brigade of a manoeuvre nature, then that brigade would not have figured within that part of the OG Bosna.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that is a fair assessment. However, I would simply point out that it was our assessment that the 3rd Corps didn't have the equipment and certainly didn't have the fuel, the petrol, as it were, or diesel in order to be able to create true manoeuvre groups that would have required transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this in fact is my next question: The 301st Manoeuvre Brigade, although it had been planned to be a part of the structure of the 3rd Corps, given the fact that the 3rd Corps had no means of staffing it and other means, that brigade existed only on paper or only in name. Please do not comment my observation, but if, for instance, you had the order of the staff of the Supreme Command of Sarajevo of 31st October 1993, where it is stated that that brigade is being dissolved and that only one tank company will be created on that basis, then your analysis made a month and a half would have created that information and not information that this is a manoeuvre company within the frameworks of the Bosna OG. Is that the way in which you wish to indicate to us the shortcomings and unreliability of the different information that you had given on the basis of this kind of analysis?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think there are shortcomings --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, this is a compound question, and it borders on testimony by my learned colleague from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript the question took almost two minutes. So your question raises a number of various matters. It would be better for you to rephrase your question by structuring it in a clear manner so that the witness is able to answer. The thesis that you wish to develop in addressing the witness is to tell him that there is a note regarding the organisation of the 3rd and 5th Corps [as interpreted] and that this report is not reliable, and if the witness was aware of an order coming from the 3rd Corps, he would not have made a very specific statement contained in this document. So it would be better to put to him a simple question, instead of making a lengthy speech of two minutes which the witness cannot follow without having all the elements in his possession. So could you put the question again in a way that everyone can follow and for the witness to be able to answer clearly. I give you the floor, Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I do apologise for this, which is my fault. In fact, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm just following your answer that the sources of information were not always reliable and that in that period of time had you had more reliable sources your conclusions would reflect those more reliable sources. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have in front of me an order by the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina which has not been translated into English because I had not intended to tender it into evidence. But I have given a copy to the interpreters for them to be able to translate my question to you. The question is the following: Had you in November 1993, when this document was compiled, had the order of the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 21st of October, 1993, in which under paragraph E it says that "a tank company of the 3rd Corps command is being formed on a provisional basis and the proposal will be drafted and submitted to this headquarters for adoption," and in paragraph K, on page 2, it is stated that "the 301st Motorised Brigade is being disbanded and all elements of its mobilisational development are being abolished"; in that case, you would have not concluded in your analysis that the 301st Motorised Brigade was part of the operations group mentioned here. Is that what you wanted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I see Mr. Mundis on his feet. But as far as we are able to understand the question, the Defence is telling us that there is an order drafted on the 21st of October, 1993, which makes mention of the fact that the 301st Motorised Brigade no longer existed, it is being disbanded; and that in those conditions why is it that this subsequent document still mentions the existence of the 301st Brigade. So the question a simple one: If the witness had been aware of this order of the 21st of October, would he have mentioned the continued existence of the 301st Brigade? Is that the gist of the Defence's question? Mr. Mundis, what is your objection regarding this question which appears to me to be quite sensible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's two grounds for the objection, Mr. President. In the first place, the witness has already said that if he had access to such documents, the assessment would have been perhaps different. So the question in that sense has been asked and answered. But second of all, the Prosecution is objecting to the way in which the question was put to the witness, in the sense that my learned colleague is again testifying about a document which is not available for Your Honours or the Prosecution in a language that we can understand so that we can see precisely what this document is. There's one thing to be asking questions based on the information contained in a document or having possession of a document; it's another thing to stand before us asserting this information and to read from a document that no one else in the courtroom has access to. And I'm not saying that the document doesn't exist. I'm simply saying, Mr. President, that there are better ways to go about doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Prosecution is telling us that this document of the 21st of October is not available to anyone, but the Defence has it. You have it in B/C/S. Is that right? And you haven't had time to have it translated? Very well. We will not call in question the existence of the document, but the Chamber is going to put the question to deal with the problem. General, the Defence has indicated that in this document that you have in front of you the 301st Motorised Brigade is mentioned. Hypothetically, had you known of an order coming from the 3rd Corps which disbanded this 301st Brigade, would that -- this document then have mentioned the existence of the 301st Brigade? So the question is a simple one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. Had we been informed in any sense that the situation had changed, the assessment would have been different. This assessment is an attempt to bring together all the available information and -- in order to use it to make a sensible assessment of the organisation of the 3rd and 6th Corps. No information available to the military information officer would have been excluded. The fact that it's not here goes to show that the available -- that the information was not available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document which was drafted by Officer Brown, when he drafted that document and when he mentioned the Bosna Operations Group, 301st Brigade, 314th, 303, 318, 319, according to you where did he get that information from? Is this visual information that he observed because your soldiers and officers are on the ground and collect information on the ground and noted down that on such-and-such a day the vehicle belonging to the 301st Brigade passed going to Zenica, or is it information coming from the HVO or perhaps even from a liaison officer close to the 3rd Corps? According to you, from what source could this type of information come from? Of course, if you know; because we are asking you things about events that took place more than ten years ago and we understand that you cannot give us precise answers. But if you can answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say, if I may so, that in a descending priority of likelihood, the first and most likely source of this information would have been from ARBiH officers to one or more liaison officers at some stage during the preceding year. The second possible source of information would have been from the HVO, who had an interest, of course, in trying to characterise the ARBiH in a certain manner. And third, and probably least likely, would be observations on the ground, because in fact there were very few vehicles and most soldiers look much the same as other soldiers. So this would have been privileged information, I suspect, from conversations conducted by liaison officers and UNPROFOR commanders from within the battalion group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, am I right in view of your earlier remark as to why you did not consider all brigades to be manoeuvre units, am I right, General, if I say that for you the manoeuvre element is the element in the army which has the capability of moving around and which has all the necessary means of transportation for this and that your assessment was that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina lacked those means? Would that be one of the grounds for your conclusion as to the manoeuvre element?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The non-manoeuvre elements were the elements that held specific sectors of the front line. The manoeuvre elements were those that could be deployed to certain points around the front line in order to concentrate force in order to try to change the balance of the battlefield. To describe them as mechanised in any sense that we would understand in a Western army would be unrealistic, given the lack of vehicles and, in particular, the lack of fuel. The critical element was not so much transport for the men. The men could march; the men did march. The critical element was the transportation of the logistics support, ammunition and other weapons systems to support such a concentration of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the President of the Trial Chamber, General, you just clarified what were your sources for information, be it when preparing milinfosums or analyses of this kind. Prior to that, you also said that one of your sources were often members of the army you were talking to. Beba Salko is mentioned in this report, and if you remember, he was a member of the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall Mr. Beba Salko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reliability of your information was actually directly linked to the reliability of the information that that person gave your liaison officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The information given to us by Mr. Beba Salko was, by our standards, important but by no means the only source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 8 of this document, paragraph 8, the heading is "The 7th Corps of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In your assessment, you rely on the information given to you by Salko Beba regarding the formation of the 7th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There isn't a page 8. You must have made an error with the pagination. It's not page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be an error on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But anyway, look at page -- that is, entitled "Assessment," and then subtitled "7th Corps of Bosnia and Herzegovina," paragraph 8 and 9. Paragraphs 8 and 9 -- and 10, actually. Have you been able to find those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, according to what is stated in this assessment, Beba Salko informed you about the possibilities for the formation of the 3rd Corps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the 7th Corps, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- but he pointed out that this should occur after the fall of the town of Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is what the report says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your tour of duty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were a witness that the 7th Corps was formed. But the reasons behind its formation were not the reasons given to you by Beba Salko and on the basis of which you made your assessment in this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. At the time that he gave us the information, we reported it as he gave it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So even a source which appeared to be reliable to you in a certain period of time could with time become unreliable, or other information that you may have gained would show you that the information obtained from that source was not quite accurate; is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it's true to say that all information we were given was to some extent tainted. People do not give information to other people in a situation of a war without some expectation that it's going to create an impression on the person to whom they give it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also testify before this Trial Chamber, General, that very frequently the parties to the conflict used wartime propaganda, which after some verifications you were able to establish that they were not true; or, on the other hand, you may have relied on them considering them to contain truthful information? So were there cases of propaganda being used as a source of your information?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's very difficult to tell what is propaganda and what is the truth. But there were occasions, for example, when one side or the other would cry that there had been a massacre and where the facts, when investigated, proved to be rather less clear than the initial claim, and other examples where a party would claim a certain action had been carried out by another one of the warring parties, but in the event it turned out to be self-generated in order to gain good publicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you witnessed the fact that the HVO, for instance, on two occasions accused the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of having committed a war crime, and when you checked it out, you were not able to establish the existence of a war crime; is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were very sensitive from the beginning about the possibility of war crimes. We were in no sense experts in the investigation of war crimes, but it was my determination that my battalion would record in as much detail as it was able the facts as we saw them on the ground when and where people claimed that there had been an event that might be a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you recollect two cases: When the HVO accused the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of having committed a war crime during combat activities, and you investigated and were unable to confirm those allegations provided to you by the HVO. Do you remember that situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could refresh my memory as to the two occasions. I remember occasions. I could give you occasions. Whether they amount to a total of two or the same two as you have in mind, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, unfortunately though I had planned to put this question to you, I didn't prepare the document that I could show you, so I'll be satisfied with the -- your answer. But my next question is: Did you also receive information from the HVO that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was using chemical weapons and this was something that you also verified; and your investigation proved it to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed. I think on two occasions we investigated the alleged use of chemical weapons, and on both occasions our experts were unable to confirm that there had been any use of a chemical weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, General, you were probably confronted with a situation in which within UNPROFOR and even other international forces on the ground there were frequently contradictory informations about the same events. Were you a witness of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is an inevitable fact that information coming from different sources will paint a situation in different ways. There is also a risk that several people will compound the problem by turning a rumour into something more solid, by reporting it repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering questions from my learned friend, you said that you collected and checked mostly the information which helped you to carry out your mandate. You didn't, in fact, make any special effort to learn all the facts about the army structure or its combat plans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I said before, it was not our business to understand in complete detail the workings or indeed the plans of any of the warring parties. Our interests began and ended where those warring parties were going to influence and affect the implementation of our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The position of the 7th Muslim Brigade in some situations was described as a shock unit. General, could you explain what was the source that prompted you to come to such a conclusion? And my second question: Did you ever see the 7th Muslim Brigade in a so-called shock operation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I may answer the second question first. The answer is no, I never saw the 7th Muslim Brigade in a shock operation. To try and answer the first question, our belief was - and this was based on observation on the ground - that there were a number of brigades whose responsibilities were primarily territorial. As I said before, they were responsible for a fixed or normally fixed part of the front line, and that's where they would conduct their operations. There were other units and brigades that appeared to have more freedom of movement and to be moved around the map in order to create a concentration of force and had a shock effect. It was our assessment that the 7th Muslim Brigade was such an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, your experience tells you that this applied not only to the 7th Brigade but that there were other brigades also who were used on a broader area and in several operations and not statically to defend the front line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My experience at the moment is based on the document I have in front of me, which seems to suggest at paragraph 33 that it was our view at the time that it was only the 7th Muslim Brigade that operated in such a manner within the 3rd Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, General, in view of the mission of your battalion, would you agree with me if I say that members of your battalion were not on the battlefront and the battlefield and did not personally observe the participation of units in battle?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it's impossible to be that black and white about it. A number of members of my battalion, in particular the liaison officers who crossed the front lines constantly and under considerable risk themselves could very much describe as having been on the battlefront. They were not there all the time in the way the fighting units were, but they had a good chance to observe the effect of warfare on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an experienced military officer, you can certainly confirm that it would not be normal for a corps of the size of the 3rd Corps to have only one manoeuvre brigade.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it would be reasonable to expect there to be more than one manoeuvre brigade, but as I said, there were from the beginning very short resources available to the 3rd Corps, in particular in transportation and in heavy weaponry. And so I think it was reasonable for us to make an assessment that the corps could probably only manage one manoeuvre brigade at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my second question as well. But in connection with what you have just said, is it true to say that the HVO had available to it much greater resources in terms of weaponry and military power than the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If you would allow me the indulgence, I think that there were quite different versions of the HVO that were in evidence within the area of my battalion's responsibility. The HVO forces that were operating in the area of Prozor and further to the south in Herzegovina were notably well equipped with things like artillery and with ammunition. These were obviously things that they were receiving support from Croatia and elsewhere. The HVO in Central Bosnia, trapped within the Vitez pocket, were not in any way spectacularly well equipped. One advantage they had was an advantage that they were largely unable to use, which was they controlled the explosives factory, the Vitezit factory in Vitez. But the HVO in Central Bosnia was not, I think, any more than the ARBiH in Central Bosnia well equipped, by military standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, General, you can confirm that even the HVO in Central Bosnia had alternative possibilities of supplies, that is, violating the no-fly zone during the night weapons were delivered at night, on the one hand, and also HVO wounded were transported by plane to Herzegovina or to Split. Were you aware of such situations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was aware of reports that this was probably going on. It's very difficult - without trying to be in any way flippant about this - it's very difficult to tell what is happening on a helicopter that's flying in the dark that arrives in your area and leaves in the dark from your area. We could tell that injured people were disappearing from the field hospital at Nova Bila, but we were not in a position to confirm that there were night deliveries of weapons. There were some daytime deliveries of ammunition that were parachuted in earlier during our time in Vitez, but I think after one such delivery by helicopter by day, the situation was considered by the Croats to be too dangerous and so flights moved to the night-time. But I cannot confirm as a result what was coming into the Vitez pocket at night in these helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, even the possibility for the wounded to be transported to better-organised hospitals gave a psychological advantage to the HVO in relation to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which completely depended on the humanitarian routes. And their openness.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was undoubtedly some sense of advantage in this, but there were also limited helicopter flights supporting the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as my diary shows at one stage, UNPROFOR spotted one of these helicopters unloading a Howitzer. So I don't think that the advantage given by helicopters was all one-sided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of your testimony today, describing the area of responsibility you said that it started on the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. Is it true that you came to Bosnia-Herzegovina via Split and along the route which passed through Livno, Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. At the time, in the winter of 1993, that was the only route available to the UN and other international agencies to get into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that route from the border with the Republic of Croatia, then via Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Tomislavgrad was under the control of the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not an accurate description of it. It was under the control of the HVO as far as Prozor. Then it moved through an area that was under the control of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina around Prozor -- around, sorry, around Gornji Vakuf. And then it moved back into a Croat area when it reached the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, if I say that the entire population in the territory under the control of the BH army in the area of responsibility of the 3rd and 2nd Corps relied exclusively on humanitarian aid coming along these routes from the direction of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, that's not a correct assumption. The purpose of humanitarian aid, as envisaged by the UNHCR, was to give humanitarian aid to identified groups at risk, refugees, other displaced persons, and groups such as women and children and old people. But the United Nations was never aiming to feed the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, I think you will agree that in this area of Central Bosnia under the army's control, as well as in the area of Tuzla, which was under the control of the 2nd Corps, there was the greatest concentration of such population at risk, refugees and other populations that needed such humanitarian aid. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to speak about where the largest groupings of vulnerable persons were. You would have to ask an expert from the UNHCR. Yes, there were many in Central Bosnia, but there were other areas, such as Sarajevo and elsewhere, where there were large vulnerable populations that were entitled to, under UNHCR rules, the support from humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to intervene, Madam Residovic. The Chamber, which is keeping track of the time, has noted that the Prosecution took 52 minutes for its examination-in-chief. We ruled quite recently that the Defence together should have 50 per cent more time than the Prosecution. So theoretically you have 88 minutes and you've already used them. In view of this concern of ours, how much more time would you need? Although you've overstepped your limit. And also the other Defence counsel may have questions for this witness. So could you tell us how much more time you'll need, because the time allotted to you has already elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A maximum of 15 minutes, Mr. President. But I'll do my best to do it in less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence counsel? How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness, so we won't need any further time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Take ten minutes, then, and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, fully appreciating your answer, because I didn't have in mind the other areas that humanitarian aid went to, is it true that the only access, the only approach to humanitarian aid into Bosnia-Herzegovina was from the border with Croatia, through areas controlled by the HVO? That was the only way the aid could access Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Theoretically, it was possible for aid to come from Zagreb through Banja Luka, and through the areas controlled by the Bosnian Serb authorities. But at this stage of the war, aid was not getting in from Banja Luka through to Central Bosnia. So the only route that was available was the route through Split through Tomislavgrad and on through Gornji Vakuf on up through to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one further topic that I would like to cover with you, and for this purpose I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 379, please. General, this is a document which you sent to the chief of staff of the command for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this letter of yours, in paragraph 1 you say that Mujahedins had captured four HVO members in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, on the basis of your information, you infer that the release of two missing hostages could be beyond the power of Mehmed Alagic, the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document, dated the 5th of December, 1993, also indicates that it is not at all clear even in those days who controlled the Mujahedin units. Did you write that as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This assessment of yours was written down on the basis of information that you had received from your liaison officer from Travnik in a letter dated the 26th of November, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This conclusion was made also on the basis of a subsequent conversation with Commander Alagic, of whom you say that he did wish to assist the Popovic family but that this was obviously beyond his power. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, from the letter of your liaison officer in Travnik, it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also emerged that the operations group in Travnik also has no ability to control the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, it followed from this that the brigade commanders of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina made it clear to you that they do not have control over groups of Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't see myself here in writing having said exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you wrote down - or rather, what your liaison officer wrote down, to be precise - is that all commanders are endeavouring to avoid responsibility and the blame for what is being done by the Mujahedin. That would be more precisely what is written in that letter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. The paragraph in question mentions Commanders Alagic and Cuskic but doesn't mention anything about brigade commanders, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In paragraph 2 it says: "The operations group in Travnik have no power over the Mujahedin and there seems to have been some considerable efforts by all commanders" and I thought that that meant commanders beyond Cuskic. But if your understanding is that it applied only to Cuskic and Alagic, then I accept that that is your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, that is my interpretation of what Captain Guinness was saying. I can't put the words "brigade commander" into his text here if he didn't use them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering questions from my learned colleague, you mentioned that while you were performing your duties you were aware of the problems in connection with the HVO decision to blow up the Vitezit explosives factory. Were you confronted with such an intention on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were first aware of this when the HVO invited the international television cameras to visit the Vitezit factory and displayed or demonstrated that they had wired for demolition a number of magazines full of explosive of one sort or another. We then asked to conduct a visit and were invited along to see very similar signs of preparations for demolition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This event attracted your attention and you invested additional efforts by informing the higher command to bring their influence to bear over the HVO to give up such an intention.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct. We conducted a technical inspection by an ammunition technical officer, who was part of our team. We assessed the size of a potential catastrophe and invited our headquarters to put pressure on the HVO authorities to make it clear that demolishing the factory would be very dangerous for the civil population, as well as for the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: An event of that kind certainly fully engaged the corps commander as well and influenced him to make changes in his plans in view of the danger that you yourself identified.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea what the reaction of the corps commander was. I didn't discuss it as such with him. I did at one stage discuss it with people in the operations group headquarters in Travnik as to whether they had a plan in the event of the Vitez pocket falling and a lot of refugees coming out of the area. But the actual -- I have no idea what Commander Alagic's view was on the explosion of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, General, for you is: Would you agree with me if I say that major or significant events such as the blowing up of the factory in Vitez or some other significant events did have a major impact on the behaviour and plans of a corps commander? Normally they would affect the behaviour, plans, and engagement of a corps commander. These were events that he could not ignore.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, any re-examination now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, General, the Judges that are before you have questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I should like to ask the registrar to give you the document that you just had before you, P378. In that document which the Defence asked you at length about, the document which was compiled by Officer Brown, we have the question of the 7th Muslim Brigade at paragraph 14 and 15 and 16. There is an assessment made in paragraphs 17, 18, and 19. Given what has been said today and to the best of your recollection of that period, the 7th Muslim Brigade was constituted from what elements?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The understanding that we had at the time was that the principal component of the 7th Muslim Brigade were displaced Bosnian citizens but that there was within this grouping a group of foreign fighters, known collectively as the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it is an affirmative answer. You say that in the 7th Muslim Brigade which you described as one of displaced fighters, there were -- there was local population and foreigners as well. These foreigners, as far as you know, came from where?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was hard for us to assess exactly where they came from. As I recall, most of our contacts with them were verbally hostile, and therefore they were not the sort of people who were willing to engage in conversation with my liaison officers or with my company commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you are saying that your liaison officers actually saw these foreign elements with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's very difficult if you don't talk to someone to tell whether they're foreign or local, but these were people who were dressed and wearing beards and so forth, looking increasingly fundamentalist in their appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your liaison officers who were in contact with the ABiH when they spoke to Colonel Williams, to yourself, this particular question, did they indicate to you that those elements of the 7th Brigade seemed to them to be under some sort of military tutorship?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My recollection is that we never assumed that the 7th Brigade was anything other than a proper part of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Mujahedin elements, their subordination to the 7th Brigade, their subordination to the military chain of command, was much more difficult to assess, but our assumption was that all organisations that called themselves operations groups or brigades fell strictly within the formal structure of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you are saying that the 7th Muslim Brigade depended on the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When we arrived, the assumption was that it was at that time subordinated to the headquarters of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document, in paragraph 15 it says, and it speaks about independent units of the Mujahedin who do not belong to the 7th Brigade and that are directly subordinated to the 3rd Corps. What does that mean, militarily speaking? Is it possible that in a situation of the time, a time of conflict, was it possible to have units that escaped a link, a strong link with an entity having military responsibility? How can you explain this in military terms? Is it possible to have independent units? And if so, to whom would they answer? Could one envisage that a group of individuals could be formed and would simply escape the HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My assessment of this is that the operations groups that you see mentioned here are largely responsible, as are the individual brigades, for territorial -- they have territorial responsibilities for the operations group controlling a number of brigades within a specific area. It's quite possible to have what one might describe as an independent organisation but to have a brigade that answers not to an operations group per se but to the next level up, so -- particularly if it's a manoeuvre unit and needs to be able to be moved from one operations group's territorial area into another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, what has been indicated in paragraph 15 is that the explanation of these independent units would be that these were manoeuvring units that would displace themselves in different geographical areas but which would in case of need be subordinated to an authority which would not perhaps be the 7th Brigade but would come from the 3rd Corps nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was very difficult, I would say, impossible for us to consider that there could be a well-armed, indeed well-motivated unit such as the 7th Muslim Brigade or indeed the Mujahedin operating within the 3rd Corps area with military capabilities that was not directly subordinate to the commander of the 3rd Corps. It would seem a very curious situation to have a heavily armed group of people wandering around inside your operational area without you having them to some extent, to the greatest extent possible, under your command and control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you as a military person, you rule out the possibility that a military unit existing there could escape the control, military control, of the 3rd Corps. Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that as and if and when they were in the area of the 3rd Corps, I cannot envisage them operating in that area other than under the direct control, albeit perhaps through the chain of command, but from the headquarters of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important. What you are saying is very important. You are saying in that hypothesis of having an independent unit the headquarters would have some sort of contact with them.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There must have been. There must have been some sort of contact, if only to pass them tasking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, at paragraph 19 it is the assessment -- it is an assessment made by your battalion, in fact. In paragraph 19 you say that the 7th Muslim Brigade may be moving away from a corps manoeuvre element to that of the army. And you're saying that this has been identified in the Fojnica area, which is in the 6th Corps area. And when this was written, the 7th Muslim Brigade was under a different corps. It is the 6th Corps that you have mentioned here in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is what the paragraph says. My view as a soldier is that if it -- if the 7th Brigade or indeed elements of the 7th Brigade moved out of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and into the area of the 6th Corps, they would come under the command and control of the 6th Corps when they were in that area. And it -- for them to be able to move from one corps area to another corps area, the clear implication is that they must have been also under the control of the central army-level staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to move them from one corps's area of responsibility into another. Although it says here "the brigade," I suspect that on reflection, given that there were still elements, as I recall, of the brigade in and around Travnik and so forth and Zenica in December, that this was probably elements of the brigade that were seen in the Fojnica area, if that is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have said a while ago that when you took over your duties in November you considered that the ABiH army was well structured and that, according to you, the structure of the army corresponded to standards of other armies. Are you asserting what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I accept that that is -- that was what I said, and I do consider that it had all the structure and all the evidence of being an army in the formal sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 18 of the document, it is said that the 3rd Corps has expressed disapproval at 7th Muslim Brigade's methods. And this paragraph seems to say that the 7th Brigade seems not to obey the orders of the 3rd Corps. How is it possible within the framework of such a structured army? How can this have happened? How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I accept what the document says here. I can't argue with what the document says. I think it -- it's hard to credit that there were substantial elements of the ARBiH that were so-called uncontrolled elements. We've seen in the other document how commanders were happy to deny responsibility for things that were perhaps viewed as unpleasant, and so there's a degree of deniability going on here. But I think in a formal sense armed elements within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps should be viewed as under the command and control of the 3rd Corps, unless they can prove -- it can be proved to be otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Judges have other questions to ask, we will take a break now and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume the hearing. The Judges have additional questions to put to you, to the witness. You told us that you had met on a number of occasions the commander of the 3rd Corps. Did you meet him there where he was performing his functions, or elsewhere? Did you visit him in his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On most occasions, sir, I met him in his headquarters in Zenica, in the steelworks in Zenica. But on occasion I met him also in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the meetings that you had, was it your impression that the headquarters of the 3rd Corps and its officers were professionals, professional military officers, or did you believe that these were persons that could not cope with their responsibilities? What was your impression? As you were a lieutenant colonel at the time, you were a superior officer; what was your impression in the meetings you had with -- of the people that you met from the ABiH? What could you tell us on that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, the principal persons whom I met were Commander Alagic and his deputy, Commander Merdan. But I also met with -- often with Mr. Dugalic, who was the head of the security, and with a number of other officers in the headquarters of the 3rd Corps; only rarely with the chief of staff, Commander Mahmuljin. But on all occasions that I met with commanders of the headquarters was that they were calm, fully aware of their responsibilities, and when they made an undertaking to do something, they were scrupulously careful in ensuring that they implemented what they had agreed to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did your battalion ever assist in exchanges of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My -- I don't recall, sir. I can't say yes on the exchange of prisoner, but certainly the exchange of bodies was -- corpses of dead military persons was a regular part of the work of my liaison officers, and trying to arrange this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in other words, you're saying that your officers would help in exchanges of bodies of soldiers or of civilians who had been killed during combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This was the residual work of the commission in Turbe, which is where Mr. Beba Salko, who we mentioned before, operated. And the job of the commission there - and there was a commission that I think was then by that stage defunct in the Gornji Vakuf area - but the commissions had taken on the role of body exchanges and exchanges of refugees and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your officers, when they were present during the exchanges of bodies, did they note the state of the bodies? Did they take photos? Did they write reports on what they had seen from these bodies, and were you informed of this? And did you pass this information to the brigadier general who was in Split?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Normally when bodies were exchanged, although the young officer would be present, it was not normally a routine, as I understood it, for an inspection to be made of the bodies. These were bodies being exchanged for a largely humanitarian reason, to get them back to their families, and I think business was carried out as quickly and as effectively as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Another Judge has some questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: General, I have very few questions to follow up what you said this morning already. In the beginning of this morning, you were given a number of documents where -- in which reference was made to Mujahedin and uncontrolled elements. And then you were asked whether these issues were raised in your conversations with members of the ABiH army, and then you started to comment on the matter of uncontrolled elements and Mujahedin. I understand from what you said this morning that you had also personal conversations on the matter with officers of the ABiH army; is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did have conversations with Commander Alagic and Commander Merdan on this issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Alagic and Merdan, those were the commanders that you had conversations with, not with other commanders?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I dealt almost exclusively with Alagic and Merdan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And what was the reason for you to discuss the matter with the two commanders of the army?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: One specific area which I needed to discuss this was the theft of equipment from my camp in Gornji Vakuf. This equipment, largely ammunition, disappeared, and also a -- an armoured vehicle was hijacked in Gornji Vakuf by elements of the 3rd Corps and all the equipment, including weapons, in the vehicle were stolen. The crew were delivered back safely and slowly some of the equipment returned. When I asked how this could have happened, I was assured that this was an act by the so-called uncontrolled elements. This was not a very convincing argument, and the lack of conviction in this argument was further reinforced when some weeks later a machine-gun that had allegedly been captured by "uncontrolled elements" turned up on the front line, was captured by the HVO from a perfectly normal BiH unit. So the deniability by using uncontrolled elements, the term "uncontrolled elements" was, I think, I believe, a convenience rather than a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was it the case that every time you had some criticism to voice or some difficult questions to put to the commanders, that they had resorted to "uncontrolled elements"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. This was -- this was not the case. And -- for example, when there was a sniping incident in Gornji Vakuf which killed a Croat, a truck driver in a humanitarian convoy, the deployment of Commander Merdan to Gornji Vakuf was instant and his investigation was meticulous, and the -- it was quite clear that the 3rd Corps took very seriously what happened along the front line, even as far away as Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was the incident of Popovic also a reason for you to discuss these matters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did have a conversation with Commander Alagic about this. As I suggested earlier, it was a somewhat unsatisfactory conversation in that Alagic implied that he probably knew what had happened to Popovic, that -- and that the result was probably not going to bring any happiness. The result -- further on, later on that -- I never had a final conversation to discover what had happened to Popovic. The issue was left hanging in the air as something which was probably not something that Alagic wished to return to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But did he say to you that the disappearance of Popovic was probably due to uncontrolled elements, or Mujahedin, or ...?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was remarkably unexplicit about what had happened. He didn't wish to be pressed on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I asked it that one. I got an answer that the solution was probably not a happy one and that there might be further news. There never was any further news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And what made you think that he already knew the outcome of the case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What made me think it was his body language, which was such that he quite clearly didn't wish to look at me when he said this and he wished to move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just before the break, we have been discussing this report on the structure of the Army of Bosnia, of the Republic of Bosnia, and the Presiding Judge has put a number of questions to you in this respect on different paragraphs, notably 17 and 18. And in paragraph 18, it says: "3rd Corps has expressed disapproval that 7th Muslimski Brigade's methods." Is that something that you know from your own experience? Is it something that comes to you personally? Is it from other members of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- ten years on, I'm not sure what the basis for this paragraph is. I'm sure it was based in some reporting, but it's not obviously indicated what the reporting is there. If I may just return to the remark earlier about what was meant by a shock brigade. I think the -- the influence of 7th Muslim Brigade was largely psychological. It was the Islamic factor and in some ways this answered the HVO, which had some very extreme - perhaps "fascist" would be the best term - but very extreme nationalist groupings, and both sides appeared to be trying to frighten the normal foot soldiers on each other's -- on the other's side by so-called special groupings that might be particularly vicious or particularly effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The report uses the word "methods." And you may think of very different things when reading the word "methods." What is the meaning of the word "methods" here?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the implication of the word "methods" is that the fighting methods of these groups would be in some way more violent, more -- less humane, if you can indeed be humane. But the shock effect was greater from these units, these special units, than from normal units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you be more specific in this respect?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I may refer to an incident that occurred in December of 1993. There was a report from the Croat authorities that there had been a massacre in the village of -- I think it's called Krizancevo Selo, but it's between Poculica and Santici. It was reported by the Croats that is more than 40 Croats had been massacred. After some considerable effort and after my liaison officer had been shot at the first time he tried to go to the area, I approached Commander Alagic and asked if we could visit this village to investigate the situation. We did so, and with his full cooperation 27 bodies I think were dug up. These bodies had been very carefully buried, each one wrapped in plastic. All of them -- as I reported at the time, all the bodies were in uniform; all appeared to have died traumatically in what I took to be combat circumstances. I then asked - and there were members of the international media present - I then asked if I could visit the three survivors of this incident, and I was taken to the prison in Zenica immediately by Mr. Dugalic. I interviewed the three prisoners. The interesting thing about this was that they reported that they had been surprised effectively at dawn by a BiH unit and that through a megaphone they had been given one chance to surrender. The three men who survived had decided to take this offer. One of them had been a prisoner of the BiH the year before. The three of them indeed survived, as they had been promised, but all those others on the battlefield were killed. Now, whether this is a massacre is another story. I viewed it as a tactical success. But it -- to some extent it goes to show you that what some might call uncontrolled elements, others might describe as special units conducting an effective military operation. But I think it was -- to me it was evidence on this occasion of the 3rd Corps being quite open about its combat activities in response to a direct question. It felt it had nothing to hide and that it had conducted the operation in a -- in as decent a manner as you can conduct a military operation. And they rejected absolutely the allegation that there had been a massacre. And in my report to the UN authorities, I had to say that I could find no evidence from -- that I could see that there had indeed been a massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So this would not be something that would merit disapproval, I would say, hearing your story.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's hard to say what merits disapproval. The whole business of war merits disapproval, and so this is -- in unfortunate circumstances. But I think it was a -- when investigated, it proved to be a combat operation that was justifiable in such terms as being a reasonable way to conduct an operation. The fact that many people died was very unfortunate, but there was no evidence that we could see they had been murdered in cold blood, for example, after the end of the battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And when this part of the report continues by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saying "the fact that the brigade attracts the more extremist and violent members of the armija has resulted in it becoming almost out of control, and constantly disobeys 3rd Corps's orders," to what reality does that refer to? The same incident or to other incidents?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This report -- this assessment report predates that particular allegation of a massacre. And I'm not in any sense suggesting that the incident at -- Krizancevo Selo was linked to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I have no idea which ABiH unit was concerned with that. I read the same words, though, that you see at paragraph 18 about the allegations of it being out of control and constantly disobeys 3rd Corps's orders. My assumption, albeit ten years later, is that the main source of this paragraph was Mr. Beba Salko in Travnik, in Turbe, and that he had an extreme, I would describe, communistic view, as an old-style JNA political officer. He had a very strong view against the arrival of extreme Muslim influence in the ARBiH. So when he says that everybody's out of control, I suspect this is to a large extent the words of Beba Salko reflected in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more question, and then I shall give the floor to the Prosecution and the Defence. In answering a question from the Judge, you referred to an element that -- an event that we were not informed of but which could be of significance for the whole context. You explained that at a given point in time a vehicle belonging to the battalion was robbed and the weapons in the vehicle were stolen. Can you remember the circumstances surrounding this event? How was it possible to do that, to take a vehicle belonging to the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The circumstance is probably more accurately described in the diary excerpts that were produced in the beginning of the morning. But just before Christmas of 1993, an ambulance, a civilian-type ambulance belonging to one side or the other - and I can't remember the exact circumstances how this happened - but the ambulance I think belonged to the ARBiH and was captured by the HVO. The ARBiH -- this is in Gornji Vakuf. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina accused my company in Gornji Vakuf of being responsible for the capture of this -- of this ambulance, whereas in -- it was in no way our responsibility. It was -- I think the driver was lost and he crossed the front line by mistake. The reaction was the following day I think that an armoured vehicle that belonged to my battalion but not one with a large cannon on it, simply an armoured taxi, with a group of men at a checkpoint was hijacked by a group of BiH soldiers who were marching past it and suddenly seized the vehicle and the soldiers in it. We immediately protested, both at the company level in Gornji Vakuf and myself directly to Commander Alagic that this was entirely unacceptable, and it was on that occasion that Commander Merdan deployed extremely quickly to Gornji Vakuf and the four soldiers involved were released within several hours unharmed. The equipment - which included a lot of mortar ammunition, since this was a mortar vehicle - and I think three rifles and a machine-gun went missing. I don't think we ever saw the mortar ammunition again, but the machine-gun, as I say, despite this incident being put down by the BiH authorities as being an act by uncontrolled elements, the machine-gun turned up some weeks later, when it was captured by the HVO in the front line at a village called Here not far from Gornji Vakuf. The circumstances were such that I was somewhat suspicious of the idea of uncontrolled elements at the time, and when the machine-gun was recovered, my suspicions were perhaps confirmed in that this machine-gun had very much been put under control and had been used against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, the HVO that captured this machine-gun, it was from which unit of the 3rd Corps that held the machine-gun on the front? Do you remember that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir, the unit in question. The location was a village called Here, spelled H-e-r-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution. Following the questions of the Judges and the elements that may appear to be new to you, has the Prosecution any additional questions for this witness? I give the floor to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution just has one question arising from questions put to the witness by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, you've talked about the professional nature of the leadership within the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and also elaborated upon what's in the document concerning uncontrolled elements. In light of that professional nature of the leadership of the 3rd Corps, what steps could they have taken if in fact there were uncontrolled elements within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is my view, and it's my personal view, that there were not uncontrolled elements within the 3rd Corps. Everything that I saw and every time I asked for an investigation or we conducted one ourselves, the impression I gained was that by the time we arrived in Central Bosnia, by the end of 1993, the 3rd Corps had settled down to become a well-structured, well-led, and by its own standards, an effective organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I do have several questions for the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Williams -- I beg your pardon -- are you familiar with the principle "under control for administration"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in an area under the control of a military unit - shall we say a corps - in its area there may be units which have some sort of administrative link to that corps? They receive administrative assistance but are operationally under the control of another corps or a higher command. For instance, the Supreme Command Staff. Would that be the actual meaning of this principle?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is one definition of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to give you an example of a British unit of the Royal Marines which was situated in a location during operations and that location was the area of responsibility of your battalion, is it true that though they were a military unit they were not under the operational command and control of the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not clear if you're suggesting that there was a British unit, part of the Royal Marines, in my area, but all units that were within my area were, I considered, I was responsible for their combat actions and I would consider that any commander should be responsible for the combat actions of units operating within his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware of the principle "unit in location"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This goes beyond the scope of questions put by Your Honours to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is of the opinion that the question is directly linked because the Defence is asking the witness about the possibility of a unit that does not come under the military authority in the area. The witness has answered. And if a Royal Marines unit was operating in the area, then I would be responsible. That was his answer. And then the Defence wants to elaborate on the issue. So put your question to the witness, because this is useful. We have a general in front of us. We are dealing with a case concerning military -- the military, and we are talk about military terms, so there's no reason why a general could not be asked a question of a military nature. So Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you conferred to me the principle of under "control for administration". I'm now asking you about another principle, "unit in location".

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't know this principle as such. Maybe this is a problem of translation, but I don't know it as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to give you an example, perhaps that would clarify the principle. Actually, do you know that in an area of responsibility of a particular military unit - in this specific case, a corps - there may be units which have nothing to do with the command of that corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I accept there may be units that are not directly under the command of that corps. The point I've made before is that any unit that conducts combat operations within that corps's area needs to be under command for those operations. You cannot -- you simply cannot organise things so that you have two different wars being fought within one area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, if in accordance with this principle in the area of responsibility of a corps there may be such a group which has nothing in common with the corps command, then the corps should have information about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That would very much be my expectation that the corps would know exactly who was in its area of responsibility. If they were inactive, maybe they were resting or training, then it would still be the responsibility of the higher command above the corps to make sure the corps knew who was in its area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Williams, is the following situation feasible: That there may be small armed groups who are totally out of control of the commander of that unit? I will give you an example, because you said that you were serving in Northern Ireland. Are there certain IRA cells over there who are quite autonomous and are not even operating within IRA frameworks? Is such a situation possible?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think that Northern Ireland is in any sense a useful analogy here. The point I'm making is that there may well be small groups of people who are temporarily out of control; this is a human failing. But where we're talking about proper combat operations, I find it very difficult to accept that formed bodies of men are conducting combat operations without doing so within a proper chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, General, that when you came to Bosnia you believed or had the knowledge that the 7th Muslim Brigade was under the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I recall, our assumption was that the 7th Muslim Brigade was both within the area of the 3rd Corps and under its command at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't have any reliable evidence otherwise, you would have no reason to change that opinion of yours, would you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The situation would be constantly assessed. But unless there was new information to contradict previous information, then the assessment would probably remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as of the 8th of November, when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, until the 2nd of December, when this assessment was compiled, you personally did not receive any information which could affect the assumption with which you had come to Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The only information that I would have received in that intervening period is reflected in the assessment made in December by the military-information office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, that assessment applied to some information that existed prior to your arrival; isn't that right? Rather than information that you personally may have received during those 20 days.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The assessment is obviously not based simply on information received in the preceding 20 days. It's an accumulative process based on the whole process of about a year that the British unit had been based in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question from the Judge, you said that it would be strange for a group to exist without being assisted by the 3rd Corps. That is actually military logic. Your reply is fully in line with military logic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as a soldier and as a person with experience in the area, you will agree with me if I say that the opposite is also possible, the opposite to which military logic would tell you.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, when you were writing your letter of the 2nd of December and even today you do not know what the real situation was with regard to the existence of such armed groups; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain. I can only give you what I consider to be a sensible assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit DH73, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please remind us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could the General be kind enough to put it under the overhead projector once he reads it. It is a document of the 13th of June, 1993 which Commander Hadzihasanovic gave to the command of Bosnia and Herzegovina with regard to the behaviour of the Mujahedin in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in November you did not know of the existence of this letter by General Hadzihasanovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this letter before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will also agree with me in saying that you didn't know that the Supreme Command of Bosnia and Herzegovina in August 1993 issued an order whereby it tried to place under army control foreign warriors.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also were not aware of the fact that the Supreme Command authorised a negotiator, because the 3rd Corps could not communicate with the foreign fighters, to try and find a way to place them under control. That is another fact that you were not aware of, were you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
