utterances.text: Answering a question from the President of the Trial Chamber, you said that the logistics support for the Mujahedin for combat probably came from the 3rd Corps; however, you don't know to this day in fact where the logistics support for the Mujahedin came from. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't know where the Mujahedin's money came from, the money they used to purchase weapons or for any other purposes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me if I tell you that at the time you did not know what connections the Mujahedin had with the religious leaders in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you also did not know that the Mujahedin played -- paid the local population to join them and fight with them in their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. First of all, I'm not sure how that -- again, we've gone way beyond the issues raised by questions from Your Honour; and B, sitting here at the moment, I'm unaware of any evidence before this Trial Chamber that would support such a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you asked a number of questions related to paragraphs in the report related to the Mujahedin, and the witness answered those questions. That is the basis for me to check with the witness again that his information about the Mujahedin and efforts of the 3rd Corps to place them under control were such that his conclusions could not be considered final, and the witness has already given me several answers. I don't know whether I have gone beyond the scope within which I'm allowed to ask this witness questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that you have -- we have another five minutes left. How many more questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which will fit within the five minutes, because it's quite possible for the Prosecution to intervene again. So do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to the other questions that were raised by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you don't really know what the combat methods used by the Mujahedin were. You don't know that personally, what methods the Mujahedin used in battle in Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally never saw or spoke to Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did encounter them on one occasion, but I didn't speak to them on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me if I say that the officer who wrote this assessment was not a person who directly talked to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. His job was one level removed from the collection of information. His job was to do with assessment information that had been received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of my cross-examination, we discussed briefly your letter written in December to the UNPROFOR command in Kiseljak. In that letter, you said that the situation was extremely uncertain with respect to the Mujahedin and that they were not under control. Do you remember us reviewing that letter of yours this morning?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this letter, which came after the report that we have discussed about the situation with the Mujahedin, comments on the Mujahedin differently than the report does? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure which sequence they were produced in, But there may be differences in the assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, General Williams, even today could you agree with me if I say that in view of the actual situation other solutions and other conclusions could be made in relation to those contained in the mentioned report?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There are always possibilities of different interpretations of the facts. I stand -- I still support the assessment made by my staff, which I believe was a reasonable assessment based on the limited information available to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, those informations did not give you a chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic, try to conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That information did not give you a chance to make a different conclusion in December; is that right? Just tell me, please: Did you ever see an order of the 3rd Corps addressed to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question, please: Can you today confirm without a shadow of a doubt that the Mujahedin were under the effective control of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I only have a few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: General Williams, you said in response to questions from Their Honours that the command-and-control situation was easier to assess between the formal units in Central Bosnia but it was more difficult to assess with regard to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And the reason for that, would it be that, as you've said on a number of occasions, you lacked hard intelligence about the subordination structure with respect to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Turning to Prosecution Exhibit 378, then, which you were asked questions about by Their Honours. Paragraph 15, if you could open up the report kindly to that paragraph. First -- the first general statement there that the "Mujahedin are subsumed within the 7th Muslim Brigade," you would agree with me that that general statement is subject to the remarks that you've made now?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the statement made in paragraph 15 may be a little too concrete, given the evidence that was probably available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, in the rest of the paragraph there is a caveat of some sort which says that there are "some independent Mujahedin units" that do not belong to the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would one of the reasons for that assessment be, as is stated in the rest of the paragraph, that there was some previous confusion regarding the dress of different armed units?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think this was a far-from-conventional battlefield, as it were, where orders of dress and the finer points of uniform were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. You said earlier on in your testimony that it was difficult to tell soldiers apart on the field.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And another reason for this conclusion in paragraph 15, would it be that there was information at the time of a separate independent unit called the El Mujahed unit, which consisted of foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: A lot of information in fact was gathered for these reports before you arrived in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Turning to the following paragraph, paragraph 16, there is information there that there was an attempted assassination on Mr. Kubura, the commander of the 7th Brigade. Did you know about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, other than what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Did you know that there were substantial frictions between the commanders of the local Muslims and the foreign Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I seem to recall that this was a topic of conversation, but I can't give you any detail on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that much of what was in this report was indeed information that had been gathered by others before you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Certainly in the case of information from July, as is clearly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You don't feel competent to talk on incidents that occurred before you arrival, I would expect.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Finally, you say you never met Mr. Amir Kubura. Did you ever meet anybody from the 7th Brigade in the command structure or go to their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of having done so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any additional questions? It is five minutes over time and there's another hearing after us. I have to remind you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one question arising from the re-cross-examination, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Williams, you mentioned in response to a question from Madam Residovic that due to human failures there could be small groups of people who were temporarily out of control.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you do as a commander when faced with such small groups of people who were temporarily out of control?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, clearly you make the very quickest attempt possible to bring them back under control to get the situation back under control, and this was very much a feature, for example, this incident in December when the vehicle was hijacked and the very commendable and rapid response from the 3rd Corps headquarters and the deployment of Commander Merdan to seize control of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Williams, we come to the end of your testimony. We thank you for coming from afar to testify in The Hague. We are grateful to you for answering questions from the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges. We wish you a happy journey home. And I'd like Madam Usher to escort you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution withdraws its tender of Prosecution Exhibit 107, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have to remind the Chamber that there was a document used during the cross-examination of the witness. This document has no status. It was not given a number Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for identification purposes. I just wanted to ask what your instructions are to the Defence, because we really do wish to produce that document and we don't know what we should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wish to produce that document during a future testimony, or you have no other opportunity to produce it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The document is the letter. And even if we had another occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please remind us which document you're talking about, because there are so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone. We are going to give this document a number to be marked for identification because there are still some outstanding questions relating to that document. Give us a number, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... DH128 [Realtime transcript read in error: "DH28"]. Your Honours, for the record, this document was used with witness Eminovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's DH128. Because on the transcript it says "28."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honour, 128.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor regarding the witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can we please for this purpose go into private session, since I'm going to name the witnesses' names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
